newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Little-known U.S. operative wields right-wing power.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Little-known U.S. operative wields right-wing power.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
When Gary Bauer speaks, hundreds of thousands of American Christian conservatives sit up and take notice. So does the Republican Party.

Little known outside conservative and evangelical circles, Bauer heads the Family Research Council, which engages in a ceaseless battle against the forces of liberalism and in defence of what he calls the "traditional family." Bauer says the rot began with the sexual revolution in the 1960s and '70s, a time when traditional American institutions were also undermined by the Vietnam War and the Watergate scandal.

"Many of the people who were part of all that in the sixties are now adults in our universities, they are professors and in the high ground of American culture where attitudes are moulded," Bauer told Reuters.

"They promote a philosophy that mocks virtue and says the right of each individual to do what they want is the definition of America, whereas our founders said that only a virtuous people can remain free," he said. "It's a very clear debate between two world views and I'm absolutely convinced that the future of the republic depends on the outcome."

Fired by religious and political zeal, Bauer reaches out to his audience with an endless stream of policy papers and a daily two-minute radio commentary broadcast on hundreds of mainly Christian stations around the country.

Bauer, who served in the White House and the Department of Education under President Ronald Reagan, has built the Family Research Council into a powerful organisation with an annual budget of $13 million, sustained by the donations of 350,000 people in the past two years alone.
SAYS PEOPLE TRUST HIM

"There are a certain number of people around the country who have vested a certain amount of confidence in me. So when I say that a particular bill is bad or good, we have found that can generate quite a bit of mail and phone calls to Capitol Hill," Bauer said.

When he mobilises his forces for a crusade, as he has done on issues like abortion, tax breaks for families and school choice, his supporters respond. "We have literally ... repeatedly shut down the Capitol Hill switchboard and the White House switchboard," he said.

Last year, Bauer was instrumental in all but wrecking the once promising campaign of Texas Sen. Phil Gramm for the Republican presidential nomination. Gramm was openly appealing for the votes of Christian conservatives, but Bauer thought the Texan was paying insufficient attention to moral issues, including abortion.

In a meeting with Bauer and some other prominent Christian leaders, Gramm refused to change his ways, saying he was running for president, not preacher. When word of the meeting got out, Christian conservatives were outraged and Gramm's campaign never recovered.

Bauer sees the Republican Party in a transitional stage, with Christian evangelicals the single largest and fastest-growing faction, though not yet an absolute majority. At last year's Republican National Convention he said he felt at home with the common folk on the convention floor but ill-at-ease with the fat cats in the VIP lounge.
MORAL ISSUES KEY TO REPUBLICAN FUTURE

"When I would go to the cocktail parties, I usually felt very uncomfortable with the people I was with because they were what is generally described as 'Country Club Republicans,' more interested in the marginal tax rate they happen to be paying than the issues I think are the future for the party," he said.
In Bauer's view, if the Republicans ever nominated a supporter of abortion rights for president the party would instantly disintegrate.

"The moment they did it, the Republican Party would cease to exist in modern American politics in the form we know it now," he said. "I have absolutely no doubt there would be a massive walkout from the party that would doom it to minority status for many, many years."

The council reserves its strongest language for its campaign against homosexuality. It opposes the adoption of children by homosexuals and campaigns hard against same-sex marriage. A position paper from the organisation bluntly states that homosexuality is "unhealthy, immoral and destructive to individuals, families and societies."
"From a religious sense, I do see it as a sin obviously, but no worse than any other sin," Bauer said.

"What causes that debate to get emotional and unpleasant is that this is a sin that has organised itself and is demanding to be treated as if it's no different than the other ways in which people choose to live."
